label: Heron
context: Heron is an iOS application designed to address the challenge of scattered hazard data faced by utility crews, as outlined in the PlanIT Control challenge from Sperry Tech. The application provides a unified view of potential hazards around job sites, including weather conditions, extreme heat, lightning strikes, flooding, wildfire risk, soil saturation, and wildlife sightings. Heron's architecture is a blend of backend services and a native iOS frontend. The backend, built using Python and FastAPI, serves as a REST API and WebSocket server, backed by a PostgreSQL database for persistent storage. Data intake is handled by Python pollers that pull weather and National Weather Service alerts, publishing them to Apache Kafka for asynchronous processing. A transformer validates and derives features from the ingested data, while a scoring service runs an XGBoost model to generate a hazard index (0-10) for each site. An alert service manages notifications, triggering stop-work alerts for lightning strikes and flood warnings. The iOS frontend, developed with SwiftUI and MapKit, provides an interactive user interface for visualizing hazard levels, receiving alerts, and reporting new hazards. The XGBoost model, trained on historical weather and incident data across Florida and the rest of the US, achieves approximately 60% accuracy, outperforming a baseline Maia model. The model's training process involved splitting data by time to avoid leakage and carefully checking calibration. The system's data flow begins with the ingestion of weather data and National Weather Service alerts, followed by feature engineering and model scoring, culminating in interactive in-game replay and AI commentary delivered to the iOS app. The team, consisting of two individuals, built a pipeline that delivers live weather data to a scored hazard level within the app, with a model that demonstrates a 90% improvement over a historical average baseline. The project's codebase comprises 168 source files, reflecting a significant effort in data engineering, model development, and application development. Heron's design emphasizes real-time responsiveness, with WebSocket connections for live updates and a single-command orchestration for deployment, demonstrating a commitment to both functionality and operational efficiency. Future development plans include retraining the model with crew reports, piloting the system at a real job site, adding offline functionality, expanding data sources, and implementing an audit log for compliance and review.
